unit-m4u3.title: Unit 4 · Lesson 3: Model Multiplying a Decimal by a Whole Number
unit-m4u3.source: enVision Topic 4 Student Edition practice pages — multiplying decimals (Drive)

summary.text: Lesson 4-3 practice pages: using place-value blocks, repeated groups and shaded grids to multiply a decimal by a whole number, deciding whether a product is less than the whole number, and using an estimate to find a misplaced decimal point.

why.text: Seeing the groups is what makes the rule in lesson 4 make sense: the digits multiply like whole numbers, and the size tells you where the point goes.

objectives.text: Model multiplying a decimal by a whole number with blocks or a grid
Regroup hundredths as tenths and tenths as ones
Tell whether a product is less than or greater than the whole number
Use an estimate to find a misplaced decimal point

parentNote.text: Built from the lesson 4-3 practice pages in her Unit 4 folder, read for what they ask. The numbers are fresh, not the page's own. Every wrong option on a worked product comes from a named slip: the point left out, the point one place too far either way, adding instead of multiplying, or writing each place's product side by side without regrouping (4 × 1.36 as 4.1224). One question mirrors the page's own critique, a product about ten times too big. Her class teaches this unit after Unit 5.

nextUp.text: Picture the groups, multiply as whole numbers, then use the size of the answer to place the point.

cards.def:
**Decide which block is 1 first: if a flat is 1, a rod is 0.1 and a small cube is 0.01.**
• 10 cubes make a rod; 10 rods make a flat.
cards.hint: Pick the one, then the rest follow.

cards.def:
**Trade 10 hundredths for 1 tenth, and 10 tenths for 1 whole.**
• 4 × 0.36: 12 tenths and 24 hundredths regroup to 1.44.

**On a 100-square grid that stands for 1, each square is 0.01.**
• Shade 25 squares 3 times: 3 × 0.25 = 0.75.

**A whole number times a decimal less than 1 gives a product less than the whole number.**
• 7 × 0.6 = 4.2, less than 7.
cards.hint: Less than one whole, so less in all.

cards.def: **Multiply as if there were no point, then place the point: 4 × 1.36 → 4 × 136 = 544 → 5.44.**

**Round the decimal, multiply, and compare. An answer ten times too big means the point slipped.**
• 7 × 0.896 is near 7, so 62.72 is wrong.
cards.hint: An estimate catches a slipped point.

cards.def:
**Turn dollars into cents to check with whole numbers.**
• 6 × $0.75 → 6 × 75 = 450 cents = $4.50.

questions.q: In a place-value block model, one big flat square stands for 1. What does one small cube stand for?
opts: 0.01, because it takes 100 cubes to make the flat
0.1, because it takes 10 cubes to make the flat
100, because the flat holds 100 of them
questions.hint: How many small cubes fit in one flat?
steps: A flat is 10 rods, and a rod is 10 cubes.
If the flat is 1, each cube is 1 hundredth, 0.01.

ex.main: **0.01.** 100 cubes make the flat, so each cube is one hundredth. A rod of 10 cubes is 0.1.
ex.tip: First decide which block is 1. Everything else follows.

ex.main: **3 groups of 0.42.** Put together, they make 0.42 + 0.42 + 0.42 = 1.26.
ex.tip: Multiplying a decimal by a whole number is repeated adding.

questions.q: Without multiplying, is 7 × 0.6 less than or greater than 7?
opts: Greater, because multiplying always makes a number bigger
Less, because you take less than one whole, 7 times
steps: 7 groups of something less than 1 is less than 7 groups of 1.
7 groups of 1 is 7, so 7 × 0.6 is less than 7.

ex.main: **Less.** 0.6 is less than one whole, so 7 of them make less than 7. (It is 4.2.)
ex.tip: Times a decimal less than 1 makes a number smaller.

questions.q: You combine some blocks and end up with 10 hundredths cubes. What can you trade them for?
questions.hint: How many hundredths make a tenth?
steps: Trading keeps the value the same and makes it easier to read.

ex.main: **1 tenth rod.** 10 hundredths make 1 tenth, just as 10 ones make 1 ten.
ex.tip: Regroup decimals the same way you regroup whole numbers.

questions.q: A grid of 100 squares stands for 1. You shade 25 squares, three times, in three colors. Which equation matches?
questions.hint: Each square is 0.01. What is 25 squares?
steps: Each square is 0.01, so 25 squares is 0.25.

ex.main: **3 × 0.25 = 0.75.** 75 of 100 squares are shaded. 3 × 25 = 75 counts squares, not the value of the grid.

questions.hint: 6 groups of 7 tenths. How many tenths is that?
steps: 0.7 has 1 decimal place, so the product has 1: 4.2.

ex.main: **4.2.** The wrong answers come from real slips: 42 is the decimal point left out; 0.42 is the point one place too far left; 6.7 is adding instead of multiplying.

steps: 0.26 has 2 decimal places, so the product has 2: 0.78.
Check with an estimate: 0.3 × 3 = 0.9, close to 0.78.

ex.main: **0.78.** The wrong answers come from real slips: 78 is the decimal point left out; 0.618 is each place's product written side by side, with no regrouping; 7.8 is the point one place too far right.

steps: 0.09 has 2 decimal places, so the product has 2: 0.72.
Check with an estimate: 0.1 × 8 = 0.8, close to 0.72.

ex.main: **0.72.** The wrong answers come from real slips: 72 is the decimal point left out; 7.2 is the point one place too far right; 0.072 is the point one place too far left.

questions.hint: 4 groups of 1.36. Regroup as you go.
steps: 1.36 has 2 decimal places, so the product has 2: 5.44.
Check with an estimate: 1 × 4 = 4, close to 5.44.

ex.main: **5.44.** The wrong answers come from real slips: 544 is the decimal point left out; 4.1224 is each place's product written side by side, with no regrouping; 54.4 is the point one place too far right.
ex.tip: Regroup: 24 hundredths is 2 tenths and 4 hundredths.

questions.hint: 6 groups of 15 hundredths. How many hundredths?
steps: 0.15 has 2 decimal places, so the product has 2: 0.90.
Check with an estimate: 0.2 × 6 = 1.2, close to 0.9.

ex.main: **0.9.** The wrong answers come from real slips: 90 is the decimal point left out; 9 is the point one place too far right; 0.09 is the point one place too far left.

questions.q: Rafi multiplied 7 by 0.896 and got 62.72. Which estimate shows his answer is wrong?
opts: 0.896 is about 9, and 7 × 9 = 63, so 62.72 is about right
7 + 0.896 is about 8, so the answer is near 8
0.896 is about 1, and 7 × 1 = 7, so the answer is near 7, not 62.72
7 × 0.896 must be bigger than 7, so 62.72 is fine
steps: 7 × 1 = 7, so the answer is a bit less than 7.
62.72 is about ten times too big.
The real product is 6.272: the point slipped one place.

ex.main: **0.896 is about 1, so the answer is near 7.** The real product is 6.272. He put the point one place too far right, as if 0.896 were 8.96.
ex.tip: A decimal less than 1 makes the product smaller than the whole number.

questions.q: A path has 4 sections, each 2.35 meters long. How long is the path?
steps: 2.35 has 2 decimal places, so 9.40, which is 9.4.

ex.main: **9.4 meters.** 4 × 2.35 = 9.40. 94 and 0.94 misplace the point, and 6.35 adds 4 instead of multiplying.

questions.q: A town planned 3 gardens of 0.8 acre each. It now makes each garden 8 acres instead. How many more acres do the gardens take up in all?
questions.hint: Find the total area before and after, then subtract.

ex.main: **21.6 acres.** 24 − 2.4 = 21.6. 24 is the new total, not the increase, and 7.2 is the increase for only one garden.
ex.tip: More in all: compare the totals, not one garden.

questions.q: Sam works out 6 × $0.75 = $4.50. How can whole-number multiplication check it?
opts: It cannot; whole numbers never check a decimal
steps: 450 cents is $4.50, so his answer checks.

ex.main: **6 × 75 = 450 cents, which is $4.50.** Thinking in cents turns a money problem into whole numbers.
ex.tip: Cents are whole numbers. Use them to check.

steps: 9 × a number bigger than 1 is bigger than 9.
9 × a number less than 1 is less than 9.

ex.main: **9 × 0.8.** 0.8 is less than one whole, so the product, 7.2, is less than 9. Every other factor is more than 1.
ex.tip: Compare the decimal with 1 before you multiply.
